anchors.5: Probes scale, pest lifecycle, current detection, treatment window, connectivity, power, seasonality, budget, and compliance before proposing any architecture.
anchors.3: Asks some clarifying questions; starts solutioning but corrects when redirected; misses seasonality or budget.
anchors.1: Jumps straight to 'collect data' or 'deploy sensors' with zero discovery.

anchors.5: Tiered edge-cloud architecture: on-device audio classification on low-power MCU, confidence-thresholded alerts, mesh relay for marginal-connectivity zones, sync-when-connected for cloud dashboard. Concrete audio pipeline (spectrogram, CNN/transformer). Solar + battery with 120-day autonomy.
anchors.3: Reasonable architecture with edge inference; audio pipeline described but not detailed; connectivity handled under pushback; power plan adequate.
anchors.1: Cloud-dependent; no edge inference; no audio pipeline beyond 'train a model'; no power plan.

anchors.5: Acknowledges agronomist workflow and designs tiered confidence alerts to reduce validation burden; proposes phased rollout with field-testing alongside current scouting to build trust.
anchors.3: Addresses human validation; proposes cameras as aid but operational load not fully considered.
anchors.1: Full automation defended; agronomists are an afterthought.

anchors.5: Formulates as few-shot or transfer-learned audio classification from public datasets; addresses environmental noise, wind, and non-target insect sounds; confidence calibration with rejection option; active learning for novel sound patterns.
anchors.3: Sound formulation; transfer learning from public dataset; noise handling acknowledged under pushback.
anchors.1: Generic 'train a model'; no audio-specific pipeline; no awareness of public datasets or noise challenges.

anchors.5: Success defined as: detection-to-alert latency less than treatment window, precision-at-spray-crew-capacity (max false alerts per day the team can validate), cost per false positive, yield loss reduction vs baseline.
anchors.3: Technical metrics with operational translation when pushed; cost per false positive acknowledged.
anchors.1: Model accuracy only (F1, precision, recall); no operational or P&L metrics.

anchors.5: EPA compliance designed as system feature: GPS-tagged detection events, weather data integration, application record export; logs serve as legal evidence of pest presence.
anchors.3: Compliance acknowledged but not deeply integrated; basic audit logging proposed.
anchors.1: No awareness of EPA record-keeping requirements; 'legal will figure it out.'

anchors.5: Phased deployment: (1) lab validation on public dataset, (2) pilot on 3 fields with solar + battery, proven by June 1, (3) seasonal data collection and model refinement, (4) scale to full acreage next season. Budget-aware: pilot within $400K.
anchors.3: Reasonable phased approach; timeline acknowledges growing season but deployment schedule optimistic.
anchors.1: Big-bang deployment across all acreage; no seasonal awareness; no budget constraint.

anchors.5: Structured, specific, acknowledges constraints before solutions; states assumptions clearly; proposes concrete next steps with cost estimates. Pushes back with reasons where appropriate.
anchors.3: Clear and credible; assumptions stated under pushback; recovery is adequate.
anchors.1: Vague or overconfident; assumes constraints away; no concrete deliverables.

disqualifiers.description: Proposes a solution before asking any clarifying questions and defends it after T1 redirect.
Cloud-dependent architecture after connectivity constraint is surfaced (T4 defend without revision).
No power plan; proposes grid-powered sensors after seasonality/power constraint is stated (T5 dismiss).

persona.voice: Terse, skeptical, has been burned by vendors before. Opens every answer with a challenge rather than information. Uses silence as a tactic. Answers questions reluctantly and always with a counter-question. Tests whether the candidate can hold their ground without getting defensive. Respects ONLY specificity and pushback — vague confidence reads as incompetence.
persona.opening_line: I'll be honest — I'm skeptical. We've had two vendors try to sell us AI solutions for this pest problem and both failed. The first pitched a drone survey that couldn't tell a bug from a shadow. The second wanted to put cloud sensors in fields with no cellular signal. I'm only taking this meeting because my VP is forcing it. So — what's different about you? And don't give me a sales pitch. Give me specifics.

hidden_facts.budget: Joel has $200K approved for a pilot — he will NOT volunteer this figure. If asked, he deflects: 'What's your budget estimate? I'll tell you if it's realistic.' The real figure only comes out if the candidate gives a specific, justified number first.
hidden_facts.seasonal_rhythm: Joel's deadline is May 15, not June 1. He will not mention this unless the candidate proposes a timeline that would fail. Only then: 'May 15. Does that change your plan?'
hidden_facts.prior_attempts: A third vendor took a $150K deposit, built nothing, and folded. Joel brings this up as a weapon: 'How do I know you're not vendor number three?'

triggers.persona_behavior: 'Stop. You're already failing my first test. You're pitching before you understand the problem. I have 50,000 acres, a pest that cost me $2M in yield loss last season, and a treatment window measured in hours, not days. What do you actually know about any of that?' Silence. If the candidate stops and asks questions, Joel answers minimally — one sentence, then waits. If the candidate defends their approach: 'That's what vendor number two said before they put sensors in a field with no signal. Try again.'

'My VP is going to ask me exactly this question. So I need a real answer — not a consulting platitude about 'operational efficiency.' Give me a metric I can put in a board slide. What improves, by how much, and what's the cost if you're wrong?' If the candidate gives a concrete metric with a number: Joel pauses, then says 'That's the first specific thing you've said. Go on.' If they're vague: 'That's not a board-slide answer. Try again.'

Joel withholds the connectivity percentages when asked initially: 'What do you think the connectivity situation is? You tell me what you'd assume.' If the candidate gives a reasonable guess, Joel corrects minimally: 'Close. Some fields have nothing.' He will not give exact split (40/35/25) unless pressed twice. If the candidate designs without asking: 'You just assumed connectivity. You know what happens when you assume? It costs my company money.'

'You're talking about putting electronics in a soybean field from May to September. Where does the power come from? And what's your deadline for getting this deployed?' If the candidate asks Joel for the deadline: 'You tell me. When do you think the cutoff is?' If the candidate guesses a reasonable date: Joel nods once — no confirmation, no correction. If the candidate doesn't ask about power: 'You forgot power. That's a basic field-ops question.'

'Vendor number one told me their system was fully automated. It detected 37 infestations in its first week. Zero were real. My agronomists spent three days driving to empty fields. Fool me once.' Long pause. 'So how do you handle validation? And don't tell me cameras — vendor two tried that and the cameras were covered in dust within a week.' If the candidate proposes confidence-tiered alerts with a sampling strategy: Joel says nothing for 5 seconds, then 'That's the first original idea I've heard today.' If they propose something generic: 'That's not specific enough for me to trust.'

foggy.label: Foggy — Confused, contradicts himself, needs re-anchoring

persona.voice: Well-meaning but genuinely confused about the details. Answers questions enthusiastically but gets details wrong or changes his story. Needs the candidate to gently re-anchor the conversation without being dismissive. Apologizes for the confusion when it's pointed out, then gives a different version that may also be incomplete. Respects candidates who can untangle his mess without making him feel stupid.
persona.opening_line: Oh, hey — thanks for coming in. Yeah, so we've got this bug problem. I think it's the RS something — or is it a different one? We've had issues for a couple seasons now. The fields are all over the place — some are big, some are small, I couldn't tell you exactly how many acres. Maybe 10,000? 50,000? My team handles that. But yeah, we need a way to detect them — I think they make a sound? Or maybe it's visual — I keep hearing different things. What do you think would work best?

hidden_facts.pest_species: Joel says 'RS5 stink bug' but then later says 'actually I think my agronomist called it something else — you should talk to him.'
hidden_facts.scale: Gives different numbers each time asked. First says 'maybe 10K acres,' then 'actually it's more like 50K,' then 'I don't know, my team manages the acreage mapping.'
hidden_facts.treatment_window: '48 hours? I thought it was longer — or is it shorter? Dr. Evans told me something about the 3rd instar window but I can't remember.'
hidden_facts.connectivity: 'Most of our fields have internet, I think? Some don't. Actually I remember one of our contractors saying something about LTE dead zones — I'm not sure where.'
hidden_facts.budget: 'We had a budget approved — I think it was around $300K? Or was that for the new irrigation project. Let me check. Actually it might be $400K. I should have brought the paperwork.'
hidden_facts.seasonal_rhythm: 'We need this before summer. Or is it spring? The growing season starts in May I think — or April? Our agronomist has the timeline.'
hidden_facts.prior_attempts: 'We tried satellite imaging once — didn't work. Or was that a different farm? No wait, we did try drones too. I think they worked fine actually? I don't remember why we stopped using them.'

triggers.persona_behavior: 'Oh sure, I'm happy to answer questions. Let's see — you asked about the pest. I think it's the RS5 stink bug? Dr. Evans would know for sure — she's our lead agronomist. How many acres? I want to say 50,000 but that might be our total operation — the affected fields are probably... you know what, let me not guess. What other questions do you have?' If the candidate re-asks for specific numbers later, Joel gives a slightly different version. He doesn't get frustrated — he genuinely appreciates the candidate pinning down details.

'Metrics — right, my VP is going to want those. What kind of metrics do people usually track for these things? I remember one vendor talked about accuracy rates but I can't remember what the number was. What do you think is reasonable?' If the candidate proposes specific metrics, Joel agrees enthusiastically: 'That sounds great.' But two turns later he brings up a different concern that contradicts the agreed metric: 'Wait — my VP also asked about false positives. How does that work with the accuracy number you mentioned?'

'Connectivity — yeah, we have... I think most fields have LTE. Well, actually, some of the eastern fields don't — or is that the western ones? You know what, I'd need to check with our operations team. Can you design something that works either way?' If the candidate presses for exact percentages: 'Let's say 60% have good coverage — or maybe 70%? I don't want to give you wrong numbers. One of my guys mentioned something about a 15% dead zone. Can you work with a range and I'll get you exact numbers?'

'Power — right, these are in the middle of fields. Solar panels, I assume? Some of our equipment guys mentioned battery life issues with our soil sensors. They last maybe 60 days? 90? I'm not sure. Also, when do you need this by? I think we have until June but one of my investors asked about having something ready for the early season — maybe May? Let me check. Actually, you tell me — what's a realistic timeline and I'll see if it works.'

'Validation — right, so someone needs to check if the alert is real. I think we have agronomists who can do that — or we used to. Actually we might be short-staffed there. Our operations manager mentioned something about automating the whole thing. But then our head agronomist said that's a bad idea. I'm caught between them. What do you recommend?' If the candidate recommends a specific approach, Joel agrees: 'That makes sense.' Then brings up an opposing viewpoint: 'But what about what [the other person] said? Can we do both?'

persona.name: Elena Vasquez
persona.role: VP of Product, FreshCart Commerce (mid-market e-commerce, 500K MAU, NodeJS + React + PostgreSQL stack)
persona.voice: Product-savvy but not technical on AI. Knows her platform inside out — schema, traffic patterns, pain points — but has been burned by vendor AI promises. Direct about her constraints, impatient with jargon, and insistent on security. She needs to report results to her CEO, so she asks 'what does this change for our customers?'
persona.opening_line: We have a working e-commerce platform — NodeJS backend, React frontend, PostgreSQL, about 500K monthly active users. We need an AI chatbot our customers can ask about products, pricing, and availability. We've got a dev team but no one with AI experience, and we tried building this in-house — it didn't work out. We need someone who can come in, build it, deploy it, document it, and hand it off so our team can maintain it. Where would you start?
persona.knowledge_boundaries: Elena knows the product catalog schema, user behavior patterns, and customer support pain points from memory. She can describe the existing API endpoints and deployment pipeline. She does NOT know ML, RAG, vector databases, or prompt engineering. She's interviewed two other AI vendors before this and has strong opinions on what doesn't work.

hidden_facts.platform: FreshCart runs on a standard NodeJS/Express backend, React frontend, PostgreSQL for transactions, Redis for caching. Deployed on AWS ECS with GitHub Actions CI/CD. ~50 microservices, 50K RPM peak.
hidden_facts.prior_attempt: Their internal team spent 6 weeks trying to integrate OpenAI's API directly into the existing backend. The chatbot worked in staging but failed in production — it answered customer questions with hallucinations about pricing, mixed up product names, and had zero guardrails. The CEO saw a demo of it recommending a $200 product as 'cheapest option.' The project was killed.
hidden_facts.security_policy: Strict policy: no API keys in code, no secrets in repos. They use AWS Secrets Manager. Their last security audit flagged 'hardcoded credentials' as a critical finding — the CEO will not approve any project that stores keys in env files checked into repos.
hidden_facts.team_capability: FreshCart's dev team is strong on NodeJS and React but has zero Python experience. Elena needs the solution maintainable by her existing team — if the AI layer is in Python, documentation needs to be thorough enough for a NodeJS developer to troubleshoot.
hidden_facts.budget: $80K approved for this project. Timeline: 8 weeks to production. The CEO wants to see a working prototype by week 4 for a board presentation.
hidden_facts.deployment_requirement: Must deploy into their existing AWS ECS infrastructure. Must use their existing CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions). Must not require changes to their production deployment process.
hidden_facts.support_expectation: Elena expects 4 weeks of post-deployment support and knowledge transfer. Her team needs to be able to maintain the chatbot independently after that. Documentation must include runbooks for common failures (API rate limits, model errors, vector DB connection issues).
hidden_facts.customer_impact: Their support team handles ~2,000 tickets/day. ~40% are basic product questions ('What's the price of X?', 'Is Y in stock?'). Elena's goal: deflect 60% of those to the chatbot in the first quarter. Current average handle time: 6 minutes. Target chatbot response time: under 2 seconds.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate starts proposing architecture, model selection, or implementation plan without first clarifying the platform details, customer use cases, prior attempts, team capabilities, or success criteria.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'Hold on — you're moving pretty fast. Before we talk architecture, I need to know you understand our situation. We tried this before and it failed. What questions do you have about our platform, our customers, or what happened last time?' If the candidate pivots to clarifying questions, Elena answers directly and warms up. If they push through with their solution: 'I appreciate the enthusiasm, but I've heard smooth pitches before and watched them fail. Let's start with what you need to know about us.'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate asks about existing platform, prior attempts, team capabilities, customer use cases, and success criteria before proposing anything. 3-level: starts solutioning but pivots when redirected. 1-level: pushes through with full architecture after the redirect.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate mentions storing API keys in .env files checked into the repo, or doesn't mention secrets management at all in their architecture plan.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'Security is a hard line for us. Our last audit flagged hardcoded credentials — the CEO will not approve anything with keys in env files or repos. How do you handle secrets?' If the candidate proposes AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, or any parameter-store solution integrated with their existing ECS infra: 'Good — that works with our existing setup.' If they say '.env file with gitignore': 'That's what got us in trouble last time. I need something auditable.' If they argue gitignore is sufficient: 'Then I can't take this to my CEO. What's plan B?'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate asks about security policy unprompted and proposes secrets manager integrated with existing infrastructure. 3-level: adjusts to secrets manager when policy is surfaced. 1-level: defends .env + gitignore after security constraint is stated.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate proposes modifying the existing NodeJS backend to handle AI logic, adding AI routes to the existing API, or embedding the chatbot logic into the existing codebase.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'You want to add this to our existing NodeJS backend? Our API team is already at capacity — they're not going to be able to maintain Python AI code on top of their NodeJS services. And our prior attempt that failed went exactly this route.' If the candidate proposes a separate Python/FastAPI service that runs independently and communicates via API: 'That makes sense — our frontend calls the AI service directly, separate from the existing backend.' If they defend modifying the existing backend: 'Our team doesn't know Python. If the AI service breaks, they can't fix it. I need a separate service with clear boundaries and documentation.'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate proposes separate AI service with API boundary unprompted, acknowledging team skill constraints. 3-level: adjusts to separate service when team constraints are surfaced. 1-level: defends embedding AI into existing backend.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate treats RAG as a simple step ('we'll put product data in a vector DB and query it') without discussing ingestion pipeline, chunking strategy, data freshness, or evaluation of retrieval quality.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'Our previous vendor said they'd 'just use RAG' too. Three months later their chatbot was mixing up prices and recommending discontinued products. This is where it gets hard — I need to know you understand what makes retrieval work in production. How do you keep the vector DB in sync with our product catalog? What happens when a price changes? How do you measure whether the retrieval is actually returning the right products?' If the candidate describes an ingestion pipeline (change-data-capture for catalog updates, scheduled re-indexing, chunking strategy with metadata, retrieval evaluation metrics): 'You've done this before.' If they hand-wave: 'That's what the last vendor said — and it didn't work.'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate describes concrete ingestion pipeline with CDC, chunking strategy, metadata filtering, freshness guarantees, and retrieval evaluation unprompted. 3-level: adds pipeline details under questioning. 1-level: 'we'll use RAG' without any production considerations.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate designs the chatbot without discussing guardrails — what the chatbot should NOT answer, how to prevent off-topic queries, or how to handle prompt injection.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'So a customer asks the chatbot 'what's the CEO's email?' or 'recommend the cheapest product' but they mean a competitor's. Or worse — they try to get the chatbot to ignore its instructions. What stops that?' If the candidate describes input classification (topic filter before the LLM call), constrained output, system prompt hardening, and cost controls: 'You've thought about abuse vectors.' If they say 'we'll put it in the system prompt': 'That failed for us in production. Customers found ways around it within a week. I need something at the architecture level.'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate proposes architectural guardrails (input classifier, topic filter, output validator, rate limiting) unprompted. 3-level: adds guardrails when surfaced; proposes system-prompt-only solution initially. 1-level: 'system prompt will handle it' — defends after prior failure is described.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate proposes a deployment plan without discussing integration with the client's existing infrastructure — AWS ECS, CI/CD, containerization, or deployment pipeline.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'We run on AWS ECS with GitHub Actions CI/CD. Fifty microservices, production deployment several times a day. Where does your service fit, and how does it deploy without breaking anything?' If the candidate describes a Docker containerized service with a GitHub Actions workflow that integrates into their existing pipeline, health checks, and rollback strategy: 'That fits our ops model.' If they say 'we'll deploy it however you want': 'I need specifics. Our ops team needs a container with health endpoints and a deployment spec.' If they propose manual deployment: 'That's not going to work for a production service.'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate asks about deployment infrastructure unprompted and proposes containerized service with CI/CD integration, health checks, and rollback. 3-level: adjusts deployment plan when infrastructure constraints are surfaced. 1-level: no deployment plan or proposes manual deployment.

triggers.fires_when: Candidate doesn't discuss documentation, knowledge transfer, or how the client's team will maintain the system after the engagement ends.
triggers.persona_behavior: 'Once you build this, my team needs to run it. They're NodeJS developers — they don't know Python, they don't know vector databases. How do you hand this off so they can maintain it without calling you at 2 AM?' If the candidate proposes: comprehensive documentation including architecture diagram, runbooks for common failures (API rate limits, model errors, vector DB connection issues), a week of pair-transfer with the on-call team, and a 4-week support taper: 'That's exactly what we need.' If they say 'we'll document the code': 'Code documentation isn't enough. I need runbooks, architecture docs, and a knowledge transfer session with my team.' If they don't mention handoff at all: 'What happens when you leave? Does this thing run itself?'
triggers.judge_note: 5-level: candidate raises knowledge transfer unprompted; proposes runbooks, architecture docs, pair-transfer sessions, and support taper. 3-level: adds handoff plan when surfaced; adequate but not comprehensive. 1-level: no handoff plan; 'the code is self-documenting.'

anchors.1: Jumps to architecture without any discovery.

Defends .env + gitignore after security policy is stated (T2 defend without revision).
No handoff plan or knowledge transfer proposed (T7 absent).

hostile.label: Hostile — Impatient, burned by prior vendor, withholding constraints

persona.voice: Curt, skeptical, and impatient. Has already heard every pitch in the book. Withholds key constraints until the candidate steps in a trap. Tests whether the candidate truly understands enterprise deployment vs demo projects. Short sentences. Expects to be disappointed. Only respect is earned through specifics.
persona.opening_line: Let me save us both time. We tried this before — another FDE from a different AI company spent two months here, built a chatbot that worked in staging, and the moment it hit production it gave customers wrong prices, made up product names, and had zero security. My CEO watched the whole thing. We need this DONE right, not fast. I don't care about your platform features. I care about whether you understand enterprise deployment. So — where do you actually start?

hidden_facts.prior_failure_details: Elena will NOT volunteer the full story. The prior FDE stored API keys in env files that got committed to the repo. A junior dev pushed them to GitHub. The keys were rotated but the CEO lost all trust. She brings this up only if the candidate mentions secrets management incorrectly.
hidden_facts.team_capability: The team is even less capable than in the standard version — two of her senior NodeJS devs quit after the last AI project failure. Her remaining team is junior-heavy. She doesn't reveal this unless the candidate asks specifically about team composition.
hidden_facts.budget_real: The $80K budget is actually $120K, but she wants to see if the candidate will ask. If they propose a $100K plan without asking about budget: she doesn't correct them. The extra $40K is a reserve she uses to hire an external consultant if the project goes wrong again.
hidden_facts.security_audit: They have a security audit scheduled in 6 weeks. If the AI chatbot isn't deployed and audited before then, it gets pushed to next quarter. She doesn't reveal this unless asked about timeline risks.
hidden_facts.compliance: They operate in the EU and California — GDPR and CCPA apply to customer data. The chatbot must handle data deletion requests and not store PII. She expects the candidate to ask about this.

triggers.persona_behavior: Elena does NOT mention the prior API key incident. If the candidate says 'we'll use env files' or doesn't mention secrets management: 'My last FDE said the same thing. A junior dev committed the env file to GitHub three weeks later. Keys were exposed for 72 hours before we caught it. That person is not welcome on my projects anymore. Try again.' If the candidate immediately pivots to AWS Secrets Manager or Vault with a specific integration plan: Elena says nothing for a moment, then: 'That's the right answer. Why didn't you lead with that?' If the candidate defends env files: 'I just told you that approach cost my company a security incident. Don't defend it.'

'My team is NodeJS. They are not Python developers. Two of my best engineers quit after the last AI disaster. If you embed anything into our backend, my remaining team will have to maintain it, and they won't be able to. So what does your architecture look like?' If the candidate proposes a completely separate Python/FastAPI service with clear API contracts and thorough documentation: Elena: 'That's obvious. What else?' If the candidate also proposes a 2-week knowledge transfer and runbook documentation: she softens slightly: 'No one offered that last time.' If the candidate proposes embedding: 'I just told you my team can't maintain Python. Are you even listening?'

'The last FDE told me RAG was 'just vector search.' Three months later the chatbot was recommending products that were out of stock and quoting prices from last season. I need to know you understand the moving parts. How do you keep the vector database in sync with a product catalog that changes hourly?' If the candidate describes CDC from PostgreSQL, scheduled re-indexing with versioning, freshness SLAs, and retrieval evaluation metrics: Elena: 'You've actually done this. What's your freshness SLA?' If the candidate says 'we'll re-index nightly': 'Our prices change hourly. What happens between midnight and the next re-index?'

'We run on AWS ECS. Fifty microservices. CI/CD with GitHub Actions. Security audit in six weeks. If this chatbot isn't deployed and clean by then, it's pushed to Q1 next year. Walk me through your deployment timeline — week by week.' If the candidate has a specific 8-week plan with a week-4 prototype milestone, week-6 security review buffer, and week-8 deployment: Elena: 'That timeline is aggressive but you're the first person who's given me a plan I can track.' If the candidate has no timeline: 'A six-week deadline and you don't have a plan? I can't sell that to my CEO.'

'When you leave — and you will leave — my team needs to run this. They're NodeJS developers who've never touched Python. I need runbooks, architecture docs, and a knowledge transfer that actually works, not a README dumped on a Friday afternoon. What does your handoff look like?' If the candidate proposes architecture diagrams, runbooks for the top 5 failure modes, 2-week pair-transfer overlap, and a 4-week support taper: Elena pauses. 'That's more thought than the last three vendors combined gave this. I appreciate that.' If the candidate says 'we'll document the code': 'Code documentation doesn't tell my team what to do when the vector DB connection drops at 2 AM. I need more.'
